rows.label: Outdoor toxic release (neutral or light gas)

parameters.sigma_form: sigma = a * x * (1 + b * x)^c, x downwind distance in m (Briggs urban)
parameters.stab_columns: day strong|moderate|slight insolation; night thin overcast >=4/8 low cloud|<=3/8 cloud

rows.source_ref: Briggs (1973) urban sigmas as tabulated in CCST (2015) Table 1.B-1 and Atmos. Sci. Lett. (2005) Table II; Turner (1970) Workbook Table 1
rows.source_note: Urban dispersion coefficients per stability class and the Pasquill-Turner stability table. Turner warns the table is less reliable over cities (urban nights near-neutral). Dense-gas switch (1.15) is WS9's and not sourced here.

sources.locator: CCST Appendix 1.B, Table 1.B-1 'Urban Conditions'; asl.94 Table II
Table 1, Key to stability categories, and the note below it
sources.quoted_phrase: The neutral class, D, should be assumed for overcast conditions during day or night.

rows.label: Vented gas deflagration in a room (accidental leak)

parameters.equation_low_strength: Av = C * As / sqrt(Pred), As internal surface area
parameters.c_note: Highest values inferred from tests in 18 references (0.18 to 82.3 m3); most likely propane value about one third of 0.17

rows.source_ref: Zalosh (2002) SFPE Handbook 3rd ed. pp. 3-414 to 3-416 (Swift-Epstein low-strength equation and C table); NFPA 68 (2023) 7.2.1; NUREG-1805 damage thresholds
rows.source_note: Room-scale planning values for accidental gas leaks. The 2023 NFPA 68 replaces the C table with a burning-velocity form (7.2.1.1) not captured cleanly here. Glass and house thresholds seen only via a secondary citing NUREG-1805 (Unverified).

sources.locator: p. 3-416, table of constant C (via Fire Safety Academy wiki, refs [3],[4])
7.2.1 Low Inertia Vent Closure Equations for Low Pred
sources.quoted_phrase: When Pred ≤ 0.5 bar-g, the minimum required vent area

sources.locator: damage thresholds as cited by the wiki refs [15],[16]; page Unverified

rows.label: Crowd crush (compression)
rows.source_ref: Fruin (1993, rev. 2002) The causes and prevention of crowd disasters, sections 'The view from the crowd' and 'Force'; SGSA Egress (Green Guide ch. 10); Buchmüller and Weidmann (2006) bidirectional flows
rows.source_note: Fruin: near-fluid crowd at about 7 p/m2, forces over 4500 N from bent railings, pile chest loads, guardrail tests. Green Guide maximum egress rates. Weidmann: 4 to 14.5 % capacity loss in counterflow. WS9's crush_density 5.0, onset and fatal times are not confirmed here.

sources.quoted_phrase: At occupancies of about 7 persons per square meter the crowd becomes almost a fluid mass.
forces of more than 4500 N (1,000 lbs.) occurred
82 persons per metre width per minute on a level surface

sources.locator: Bi-directional flows, Fig. 25 text and Table 15

rows.label: Vehicle strikes pedestrians (injury-risk curve)

parameters.curve_basis: average adult pedestrian struck by a car or light truck, US 2007-2009 standardised
parameters.age_note: risk at 25 mph for a 70-year-old is similar to a 30-year-old at 35 mph

rows.source_ref: Tefft (2013) Accident Analysis and Prevention 50, 871-878; AAA Foundation (2011) report abstract; NHTSA DOT HS 812 059 Table 1
rows.source_note: Risk of severe injury and of death against impact speed, stored in the source's mph (conversion is code's job). Bands only: WS9 6.27.10 offers no exact speed. Vehicle class masses and barrier classes not confirmed here.

sources.quoted_phrase: the average risk of death for a pedestrian reaches 10% at an impact speed of 23 mph

rows.label: Aircraft impact into a building (public-report planning values)

parameters.fuel_fraction_external_fireball_ncstar1: roughly comparable to the internal spray burn (under 0.15)
parameters.fireproofing_note: insulation widely dislodged in the impact zone; NIST found the towers would have stood without dislodged fireproofing and multi-floor fires

rows.source_ref: NIST NCSTAR 1 (2005) ch. 2 and executive summary; FEMA 403 (2002) ch. 8 8.2.2.1(c); NRC Canada, Role of fire resistance issues (restating FEMA 403 and Rehm et al. 2002)
rows.source_note: How fuel splits between fireball, shafts and early burning, and the role of dislodged fireproofing, at public-report level. Two estimates disagree (NIST under 15 % each; FEMA 25 %): reviewer picks. No class masses, swath, penetration or approach data.

sources.quoted_phrase: Less than 15 percent of the jet fuel burned in the spray cloud inside the building.
would have remained standing were it not for the dislodged insulation (fireproofing)
About 25 percent of this quantity was consumed in the initial blast and resulting fireball.
A significant portion of this fuel was consumed immediately in the ensuing fireballs.
